bibl.title: Building Machines That Learn and Think Like People

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: critique
span.quote: Despite their biological inspiration and performance achievements, these systems differ from human intelligence in crucial ways.

span.label: human-like learning and thinking in machines
span.quote: In this article, we view this excitement as an opportunity to examine what it means for a machine to learn or think like a person.

span.label: review
span.quote: We review progress in cognitive science suggesting that truly human-like learning and thinking machines will have to reach beyond current engineering trends in both what they learn, and how they learn it.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: PERFORMANCE PARITY IS GRANTED AND SIMILARITY DENIED IN CONSECUTIVE SENTENCES: these systems achieve performance that EQUALS OR EVEN BEATS HUMANS IN SOME RESPECTS - DESPITE their biological inspiration and performance achievements, they DIFFER FROM HUMAN INTELLIGENCE IN CRUCIAL WAYS. Matching a score is separated from being alike, and the concession comes first
span.quote: Many advances have come from using deep neural networks trained end-to-end in tasks such as object recognition, video games, and board games, achieving performance that equals or even beats humans in some respects. Despite their biological inspiration and performance achievements, these systems differ from human intelligence in crucial ways.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE CRITERION IS SPLIT INTO TWO DIMENSIONS SO THAT A SYSTEM CAN FAIL ON EITHER: truly HUMAN-LIKE learning and thinking machines will have to reach beyond current engineering trends in **BOTH WHAT THEY LEARN, AND HOW THEY LEARN IT**. One adjective, two independent requirements
span.quote: We review progress in cognitive science suggesting that truly human-like learning and thinking machines will have to reach beyond current engineering trends in both what they learn, and how they learn it.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A QUESTION IS DECLARED OLDER THAN THE NAMES OF BOTH FIELDS THAT ASK IT: the questions of whether and how AI should relate to human cognitive psychology are **OLDER THAN THE TERMS ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND COGNITIVE PSYCHOLOGY**. The problem existed before either vocabulary did, which means neither vocabulary was built to state it
span.quote: The questions of whether and how AI should relate to human cognitive psychology are older than the terms ‘artificial intelligence’ and ‘cognitive psychology.’

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE POSITION BEING ARGUED AGAINST IS QUOTED FROM A TEXTBOOK, AS AN ANALOGY ABOUT ABANDONING IMITATION: the quest for ARTIFICIAL FLIGHT succeeded WHEN THE WRIGHT BROTHERS AND OTHERS **STOPPED IMITATING BIRDS** and started using wind tunnels and learning about aerodynamics. The rival view is presented in its own strongest form, in its own words, with a page reference
span.quote: The quest for ‘artificial flight’ succeeded when the Wright brothers and others stopped imitating birds and started using wind tunnels and learning about aerodynamics.” (p. 3).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A DEFENDER'S HOPE IS GRANTED SYMPATHY AND THEN DOUBTED, WITH THE DOUBT MARKED AS UNCERTAIN: WE CAN SYMPATHIZE WITH THAT HOPE AND BELIEVE IT DESERVES FURTHER EXPLORATION, **ALTHOUGH WE ARE NOT SURE IT IS A REALISTIC ONE**. Disagreement stated as an uncertainty about the opponent's prospects rather than as a refutation
span.quote: We can sympathize with that hope and believe it deserves further exploration, although we are not sure it is a realistic one.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE BENCHMARK'S SCALE IS MADE CONCRETE BY NAMING THE OBJECTS: benchmark tasks provide HUNDREDS OR THOUSANDS OF EXAMPLES PER CLASS - **1000 HAIRBRUSHES, 1000 PINEAPPLES**, etc. - and one dataset includes 6000 examples of each handwritten digit. An abstract quantity is turned into a picture of what the quantity is made of
span.quote: Benchmark tasks such as the ImageNet data set for object recognition provides hundreds or thousands of examples per class (Krizhevsky et al., 2012; Russakovsky et al., 2015) – 1000 hairbrushes, 1000 pineapples, etc. In the context of learning new handwritten characters or learning to play Frostbite, the MNIST benchmark includes 6000 examples of each handwritten digit (LeCun et al., 1998)

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: TWO QUANTITIES A SINGLE COMPARISON CONFLATES ARE SEPARATED IN A FOOTNOTE: the time required to train the network - **COMPUTE TIME** - **IS NOT THE SAME AS THE GAME (EXPERIENCE) TIME**, and compute time CAN BE LONGER. Two clocks under one word, distinguished where a reader might not look
span.quote: The time required to train the DQN (compute time) is not the same as the game (experience) time. Compute time can be longer.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A METRIC IS DESCRIBED AS DESIGNED TO BLOCK ONE SPECIFIC CHEAT, AND ITS RIVALS' STATUS IS DECLARED UNKNOWN: the reported scores use the HUMAN STARTS measure, **DESIGNED TO PREVENT NETWORKS FROM JUST MEMORIZING LONG SEQUENCES OF SUCCESSFUL ACTIONS FROM A SINGLE STARTING POINT** - and faster learning and higher scores HAVE BEEN REPORTED USING OTHER METRICS, **BUT IT IS UNCLEAR HOW WELL THE NETWORKS ARE GENERALIZING WITH THESE ALTERNATIVE METRICS**. The number depends on which measure, and only one of them is known to mean what it says
span.quote: The reported scores use the “human starts” measure of test performance, designed to prevent networks from just memorizing long sequences of successful actions from a single starting point. Both faster learning (Blundell et al., 2016) and higher scores (Wang et al., 2016) have been reported using other metrics, but it is unclear how well the networks are generalizing with these alternative metrics.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: AN OPPOSING SCHOOL'S POSITION IS SUMMARISED AS A CLAIM ABOUT METAPHOR: proponents maintain that classic types of structured knowledge - graphs, grammars, rules, objects, programs - CAN BE USEFUL YET **MISLEADING METAPHORS** for characterizing thought, and that these structures are **MORE EPIPHENOMENAL THAN REAL**. The disagreement is over whether the vocabulary names things or describes them
span.quote: Proponents of this approach maintain that many classic types of structured knowledge, such as graphs, grammars, rules, objects, structural descriptions, programs, etc. can be useful yet misleading metaphors for characterizing thought. These structures are more epiphenomenal than real, emergent properties of more fundamental sub-symbolic cognitive processes (McClelland et al., 2010).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE OBJECTION TO THE PAPER'S OWN COMPARISON IS RAISED BY THE PAPER, EARLY, AND FLAGGED AS ANTICIPATED: one might object that both challenges draw an **UNFAIR COMPARISON** between the speed of human learning and neural network learning - discussed in detail later, **BUT WE FEEL IT IS IMPORTANT TO ANTICIPATE HERE AS WELL**. The strongest attack on the paper's method is placed before the method is used
span.quote: One might object that both the Frostbite and Characters challenges draw an unfair comparison between the speed of human learning and neural network learning. We discuss this objection in detail in Section 5, but we feel it is important to anticipate here as well.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: AND THE REFRAMING THE PAPER ADOPTS IS QUOTED FROM AN ANONYMOUS REVIEWER OF AN EARLIER DRAFT: **THEY MAY BE BETTER SEEN AS SOLVING DIFFERENT TASKS** - the human ENCOUNTERING ONE IN A YEARS-LONG STRING OF PROBLEMS WITH RICH OVERLAPPING STRUCTURE, the network STARTING COMPLETELY FROM SCRATCH. **The comparison fails not through a confound but because one phrase, `the task`, was covering two different things** - and the authors reply WE AGREE
span.quote: They may be better seen as solving different tasks. Human learners – unlike DQN and many other deep learning systems – approach new problems armed with extensive prior experience. The human is encountering one in a years-long string of problems, with rich overlapping structure. Humans as a result often have important domain-specific knowledge for these tasks, even before they ‘begin.’ The DQN is starting completely from scratch.” We agree, and indeed this is another way of putting our point here.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A CAPACITY IS SHOWN TO PERSIST DESPITE THE PRACTICE THAT WOULD EXPLAIN IT: children are FAR MORE PRACTICED than adults at learning new concepts - ROUGHLY NINE OR TEN NEW WORDS EACH DAY - YET the ability for rapid ONE-SHOT learning **DOES NOT DISAPPEAR IN ADULTHOOD**. The obvious explanation for the skill is present in one group and the skill in both
span.quote: Children are far more practiced than adults at learning new concepts – learning roughly nine or ten new words each day after beginning to speak through the end of high school (Bloom, 2000; Carey, 1978) – yet the ability for rapid “one-shot” learning does not disappear in adulthood.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE PAPER'S OWN CRITERIA ARE CALLED INGREDIENTS AND PLACED AFTER A REVIEW OF OTHER PEOPLE'S: first the criteria PREVIOUSLY OFFERED by cognitive scientists, developmental psychologists and AI researchers are reviewed - THEN what the authors VIEW AS THE **ESSENTIAL INGREDIENTS** is articulated. The list is presented as a synthesis with a named provenance, not as a definition
span.quote: We first review some of the criteria previously offered by cognitive scientists, developmental psychologists, and AI researchers. Second, we articulate what we view as the essential ingredients for building such a machine that learns or thinks like a person, synthesizing theoretical ideas and experimental data from research in cognitive science.

span.label: planning in complex (model-based) systems is cumbersome and slow for real-time control
span.note: what this limits: the real-time control claim: PLANNING IN COMPLEX MODELS IS CUMBERSOME AND SLOW
span.quote: planning in complex models is cumbersome and slow

span.label: The article says very little about natural language, a capacity the authors concede is central to human intelligence.
span.note: what this limits: the scope of the whole article: WE HAVE SAID LITTLE ... ABOUT PEOPLE'S ABILITY TO COMMUNICATE AND THINK IN NATURAL LANGUAGE, A DISTINCTIVELY HUMAN COGNITIVE CAPACITY WHERE MACHINE CAPABILITIES LAG STRIKING[ly]
span.quote: We have said little in this article about people’s ability to communicate and think in natural language, a distinctively human cognitive capacity where machine capabilities lag strikingly.

span.label: The proposed list of core ingredients is explicitly not claimed to be complete.
span.note: what this limits: the list of core ingredients: WE DID NOT INTEND OUR LIST TO BE COMPLETE
span.quote: These are important questions for future work with the potential to expand the list of key ingredients; we did not intend our list to be complete.

span.label: The authors concede the objection that humans bring far richer prior experience to a new task than a network does, which complicates the learning-speed comparisons the paper rests on.
span.note: what this limits: the human-machine comparison: humans bring far richer prior experience to a new task than a network does, which the authors concede as an objection
span.quote: We agree that humans have a much richer starting point than neural networks when learning most new tasks, including learning a new concept or to play a new video game.

span.label: Their own prior model of the Characters Challenge does not capture the full human ability.
span.quote: We recently reported progress on this challenge using probabilistic program induction (Lake, Salakhutdinov, & Tenenbaum, 2015), yet aspects of the full human cognitive ability remain out of reach.

span.label: Equal performance on the benchmark is stated not to indicate equal capability.
span.note: what this limits: any comparison of human and network ability based on these benchmarks: the authors state that performing equally well on MNIST and other large-scale image classification tasks does not mean humans and networks learn and think in the same way
span.quote: While humans and neural networks may perform equally well on the MNIST digit recognition task and other large-scale image classification tasks, it does not mean that they learn and think in the same way. There are at least two important differences: people learn from fewer examples and they learn richer representations

span.label: The human-level comparison is stated for specific data sets, with one described as within reach rather than reached.
span.note: what this limits: any claim that networks have matched human performance: the authors report an error rate very close to human-level on one task and describe human-level performance as within reach on the ImageNet benchmark
span.quote: The best results achieved using deep convolutional nets are very close to human-level performance at an error rate of 0.2% (Ciresan, Meier, & Schmidhuber, 2012). Similarly, recent results applying convolutional nets to the far more challenging ImageNet object recognition benchmark have shown that human-level performance is within reach on that data set as well

span.label: the list of differences - A FLOOR, NOT A SET: the authors write that there are AT LEAST two important differences before naming two, so the enumeration is explicitly open and a reader who treats the two as the complete account has closed a list the authors left open
